transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-09-01 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Mark Liu (CumulusHealth CTO), Jamie Ortiz (Eng PM), Samantha Green (Frontend Eng), Evan Park (SRE)

Summary: quick hosted API walkthrough focused on streaming handshake, timeout patterns, retry/backoff, and console tips for performance observability. Customer cares about low-latency chat, predictable tail-latency, and HIPAA-sensitive data paths.

[00:00] Alex: all right, hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm alex from redwood, um priya and diego are with me, we'll run through a short hosted demo focused on streaming behavior, handshake, timeouts, and some retry patterns. can you confirm audio/video ok?
[00:12] Mark: yep i'm good, thanks. sorry if background noise, been hopping between meetings.
[00:18] Priya: great. quick agenda — 1) small API demo, 2) console observe/trace example, 3) talk through retries/backoff and recommended params, 4) q&a and next steps.
[00:31] Jamie: sounds good. our biggest open questions are: how do we keep 95th percentile under 350ms for short chat completions, what do streaming handshakes cost, and how to debug partial responses.
[00:44] Diego: perfect thanks. one quick note: we'll reference a short deck and the sandbox creds — links at the end of the call.

--- API demo / handshake timeline ---
[01:05] Priya: ok i'm going to run a very small request live against the hosted chat endpoint. this is basically a two-turn prompt, short completion so you can see the streaming tokens come in.
[01:20] [Priya shares terminal, types curl sample] 
[01:28] Priya: here's the call: POST /v1/chat/completions, stream=true, model=redwood-rl-small (demo model), messages payload, and we set a client-side read timeout of 10s.
[01:41] Samantha: quick q — what do you mean by handshake? are there extra rpcs before tokens stream?
[01:46] Priya: good question. handshake is mostly the http request/response startup — the server sends an initial HTTP 200 and then starts chunked transfer. real-time latency depends on kernel warmup and kv cache hit. sometimes folks call it the 'stream handshake' because you wait for the first chunk.
[02:05] Mark: kv cache? heard of K V cash earlier, can you spell that?
[02:10] Diego: yeah it's K-V cache, the key/value cache for attention states — sorry transcription may show K V cash in notes.
[02:18] [00:02:30] Priya: streaming demo — tokens appear every ~30-60ms per chunk for this short sample. if you set smaller max_tokens or top_p that can affect how many chunks you get.
[02:35] Priya: note: if the client read timeout is too aggressive you will see an abrupt connection close and partial output. for example we see some customers set 2s timeouts and get truncated responses on bursty inputs.

--- Console and traces ---
[03:05] Diego: switching to console — i'll show how to find the request trace, you can see token-level breakdown, model variant, kernel selected, and whether prefix caching hit.
[03:22] [Diego screenshares console, clicks into a request] 
[03:30] Diego: here you can filter by model, by route, or by customer token. the console will show a latency waterfall — DNS, TLS, model-queued, model-exec, and streaming bytes. that helps isolate tail latency.
[03:48] Evan: can we see client-side RTT vs server exec separately?
[03:52] Diego: yes — request shows both. one caveat the console's RTT is based on our edge instrumentation; if you have complex internal networking (VPNs/proxies) account for that.

--- Retries, idempotency, and timeouts ---
[04:25] Priya: common patterns: 1) optimistic short read timeout + retry with exponential backoff, 2) prefer idempotent pattern on server side; we support idempotency keys per request so replays avoid dup billing or duplicate side effects, 3) streaming resume vs full retry — currently we don't support stream resume on hosted, so a retry issues a new request from scratch.
[04:55] Jamie: that stream resume piece is important — so if a user loses connection they have to re-request and tolerate repeat tokens?
[05:03] Priya: yes correct. you can implement client dedupe by passing idempotency keys and tracking last server partial chunk if you need to avoid duplication in your UI.
[05:15] Mark: how does that interact with caching? if we re-request a short prompt, will kv cache help and reduce exec time?
[05:22] Diego: absolutely, kv cache hits can reduce model-exec time a lot for conversational context. repeated short prompts with same prefix often hit the cache. quantization and model variant also matter.

--- Backpressure and batching notes ---
[05:45] Priya: for bulk scenarios where you need throughput, we recommend batching at the client or using Redwood Dedicated pools. Hosted has automatic batching but it's tuned for latency-sensitive workloads, so throughput-focused customers often pick Dedicated.
[06:05] Samantha: curious on cost: if we get batching on hosted does that reduce per-token cost?
[06:10] Diego: yes batching and prefix cache reduce per-token GPU compute; Optimize can recommend batching configs given observed traffic. we'll include sample numbers in the follow-up.

--- Real-world failure modes ---
[06:40] Priya: common failure modes we see in customers: 1) too-short client read timeouts, 2) insufficient retry backoff (aggressive retries amplifying load), 3) misconfigured concurrency leading to queued requests, 4) forgetting to set idempotency keys causing duplicate side-effects.
[06:59] Evan: we have autoscaler rules and can adjust from infra side, but want to know how Redwood surfaces queued vs throttled requests in the console.
[07:08] Diego: console shows queueing metrics and a per-model queued count; we also emit alerts if queue depth crosses thresholds.

--- Security/compliance quick Qs ---
[07:35] Mark: two quick security items — HIPAA and SSO. can you confirm hosted supports customer KMS for encryption at rest?
[07:44] Alex: hosted supports customer-managed keys for Private; for pure hosted we offer encrypted storage and SOC2 cert, but customer-managed KMS/HSM is part of our Private offering (VPC/on-prem). we'll send the security pack with network diagram.
[08:00] Mark: okay and SAML/SCIM provisioning?
[08:05] Alex: yes SSO via SAML, SCIM for provisioning, RBAC. full details in the security doc we'll share.

--- Q&A and live troubleshooting scenario ---
[08:30] Jamie: let's simulate a frontend user losing connection mid-stream. how should our client behave?
[08:36] Priya: recommended flow: show partial output as it arrives; on a disconnect, attempt a single backoff retry with same idempotency key. if you expect duplicates in UI, dedupe by token offset or a server-generated message id we include in response metadata.
[08:58] Samantha: is there a message id field in the streaming chunks?
[09:02] Priya: yes each chunk includes a small metadata envelope — note sometimes our transcript will show it as chunk-id but it's actually message_id. we'll include the sample response schema in follow-up.

[09:20] [09:20] Diego: quick note on timeouts — network-level timeouts vs application read timeouts differ. for node clients set socket timeout higher than your UI spinner threshold and use streaming keep-alives so the browser connection doesn't think it's dead.

--- Deeper on parameters ---
[10:00] Priya: parameters we often tweak for latency vs quality: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stream_chunk_size. also look at model variant (e.g., redwood-rl-small vs redwood-rl-large) and quantization. lowering max_tokens reduces total streaming time, of course.
[10:22] Mark: any rule-of-thumb for chunk sizes?
[10:25] Priya: we typically surface token-chunk frequency rather than bytes. for chat UIs, aim for 20-40 token chunk windows to give smooth UX; if chunks are too small you increase HTTP overhead.

--- Console Optimize suggestions ---
[11:10] Diego: i'll bring up Optimize recommendations — we ran a sample on one of your public repos (demo dataset) and Optimize suggested a mixed strategy: pinning a medium-latency model for 95% of traffic and fallback to a cheaper quantized variant for non-latency-critical batches. also suggestions for caching prefixes for common prompts.
[11:33] Mark: that pin strategy — does Redwood do automatic routing/fallback?
[11:37] Diego: yes, Smart Routing lets you route requests by latency or cost policy, and can fallback automatically to pinned variants if primary capacity constrained. we'll include sample configs in the docs.

--- Handshake timing numbers (live) ---
[12:05] Priya: just ran three samples — cold-start handshake ~420ms, warm handshake ~120ms with kv cache, first token ~30ms after handshake on warm path. note these numbers are for short completions on our EU region, your numbers may vary depending on peering.
[12:28] Evan: interesting, our target is 350ms 95th so warm path looks promising but cold starts might be trouble during spikes.
[12:36] Priya: to reduce cold starts we recommend pre-warming via a lightweight synthetic traffic or using Dedicated for guaranteed warm instances. also can increase burst capacity config.

--- Billing/Token accounting note ---
[13:05] Alex: small billing nuance — retries that start new requests may generate additional token billing if the model produces tokens before you stop. idempotency keys don't prevent token billing on replays; they prevent duplicated external side-effects.
[13:22] Mark: good to know, we'll plan conservative retry budgets.

--- Live spike scenario — throttles and graceful degradation ---
[14:00] Priya: if you hit quota or throttle, recommended fallback is to degrade to a smaller model or synthetic canned responses for non-critical messages. Console can auto-route to a fallback variant.
[14:18] Jamie: can that be per-route? for example search vs chat?
[14:22] Diego: yes routes are configurable. you can set per-route SLOs and fallback model mapping.

--- Customer concerns / misc ---
[15:05] Mark: latency aside, we also need obvious audit logs for compliance — can you show how audit logs look?
[15:12] Diego: navigate to the audit tab — we log request create, model selection, rollouts, and admin auth events. we'll provide the schema in the security pack.

--- Minor transcription glitches acknowledged ---
[15:40] Alex: note — the auto-transcript may spell some acronyms weirdly (e g K V cache / SAML) we'll attach a cleaned cheat-sheet.

--- Closing and recap ---
[16:00] Alex: OK quick recap — we showed a live streaming chat demo, explained handshake vs token stream, touched on console traces, talked about retries/idempotency and billing nuance, and outlined options to reduce cold starts (pre-warm, Dedicated, burst config).
[16:20] Alex: next steps are the ones we captured: we'll send pricing, security docs, a short console walkthrough video, and set up an E2E latency POC.
[16:33] Mark: thanks — that's helpful. we'll prepare the prompt set and internal SRE contacts for the POC.
[16:40] Jamie: one last ask — can you include an example node client snippet showing socket and read timeout recommendations?
[16:46] Priya: yes we'll include that in the follow-up plus a sample dedupe pattern using idempotency keys.
[16:55] Alex: great. thanks everyone, we'll follow up by email this week.
